description.short_caption: Erythematous maculopapular rash on the legs.
description.detailed_description: This clinical photograph shows the lower legs of a patient with a diffuse erythematous maculopapular rash. The rash is evenly distributed and involves both legs symmetrically. The skin appears otherwise intact without evidence of ulceration, vesicles, or purpura. The image is taken in a clinical setting with the patient lying down, and a blue drape is partially visible.

description.short_caption: Diffuse maculopapular rash on the torso.
description.detailed_description: This clinical photograph shows the anterior torso of a patient with a diffuse maculopapular rash. The rash consists of numerous small, red macules and papules distributed across the chest and upper abdomen. Electrocardiogram (ECG) leads and a blood pressure cuff are visible, suggesting the patient is being monitored in a clinical setting. The rash appears non-vesicular and non-confluent, with no visible signs of ulceration or crusting.
visible_findings: ECG leads and blood pressure cuff

Case_13010/figure3.jpg.source_caption: MRI of the brain, T1 gadolinium-enhanced view.

description.short_caption: MRI of the brain, T1 gadolinium-enhanced axial view.
description.detailed_description: This is an axial T1-weighted MRI image of the brain with gadolinium contrast enhancement. The image shows symmetric enhancement of the meninges along the convexities, suggestive of meningeal inflammation or enhancement. The ventricles appear normal in size, and no focal mass lesions are evident. The gadolinium contrast highlights the vascular and meningeal structures.

Case_13010/figure4.jpg.source_caption: MRI of the brain, FLAIR view.

description.short_caption: MRI of the brain, FLAIR sequence showing cortical and subcortical abnormalities.
description.detailed_description: This is an axial FLAIR MRI image of the brain. The image demonstrates hyperintense signal abnormalities in the cortical and subcortical regions, particularly in the bilateral frontal lobes. The sulci are well-defined, and there is no evidence of midline shift. The findings may suggest inflammation, infection, or other pathological processes affecting the brain parenchyma.
visible_findings: hyperintense signal in cortical and subcortical regions
